canberra.title: Questacon leads Canberra winners bound for national tourism showdown
canberra.snippet: Grit and excellence won the day at the Canberra region’s premier tourism awards tonight (20 November), with 18 local operators prov...
canberra.content:
20 November 2026

Start the conversation

Winning the Major Tourist Attractions category in the Canberra Region Tourism Awards for the third year in a row, Questacon is closer than ever to the Australian Tourism Awards Hall of Fame. Photo: John Lomnicki.

Grit and excellence won the day at the Canberra region’s premier tourism awards tonight (20 November), with 18 local operators proving the capital’s visitor economy is thriving despite a tough economic climate.

From late-night gins at The Canberra Distillery to staycations at Little National and family days out at Questacon, Canberra’s favourite local haunts took top honours at the 2026 Canberra Region Tourism Awards.

The who’s who of the industry gathered at the prestigious Gandel Hall at the National Gallery of Australia for the event, which celebrates the businesses, attractions and experiences that make the Canberra Region a great place to visit.

Across a diverse field of entrants across a broad range of categories, Questacon stood as a major highlight, winning the category of Major Tourist Attractions for the third consecutive year, edging the beloved institution closer to the elusive Australian Tourism Awards Hall of Fame.

The hotel sector was well represented, with the Hyatt Hotel Canberra, Little National and Leumeah Lodge each taking out the win in their respective categories.

Competition was particularly strong in the Winery and Distilleries category, with The Canberra Distillery receiving the win.

Multiple award winner and previous national placegetter Alivio Tourist Park will continue its quest for national honours in the category of Caravans and Holiday Parks, while the Royal Australian Mint took out a coveted double victory, claiming both the Cultural Tourism and Tourism Retail & Hire Services categories.

Eighteen businesses will fly the flag for the Canberra Region at the Australian Tourism Awards in Geelong in February 2027.

Hyatt Hotel Canberra – A Park Hyatt Hotel took out the 5 Star Luxury Accommodation category. Photos: Hyatt Hotel Canberra.

Canberra Region Tourism Industry Council Managing Director Debra Beetham said the calibre of this year’s entrants proved local operators were refusing to let economic headwinds slow them down.

“Our tourism businesses continue to deliver outstanding experiences for visitors, even in a tough economic climate,” she said.

“I’m proud of every business that put itself forward, and it’s wonderful to see their hard work and contribution to our region recognised.

“The awards process gives operators a chance to step back from the day-to-day running of their business, benchmark their performance against industry standards and look closely at where they can improve.”

The winners of the 2026 Canberra Region Tourism Awards were:

Major Tourist Attractions

  • Winner – Questacon, The National Science & Technology Centre

Tourist Attractions

  • Winner – Canberra Reptile Zoo and Wildlife Encounters
  • Highly Commended – Blackwattle Alpaca Farm

Major Festivals and Events

  • Winner – Events ACT – Floriade 2025

Festivals & Events

  • Winner – Murrumbateman Field Days
  • Highly Commended – Parkrun Canberra Region

Ecotourism

  • Winner – Wildlife Reimagined

Cultural Tourism

  • Winner – Royal Australian Mint

Tourism Retail, Hire and Services

  • Winner – Royal Australian Mint, The Mint Shop
  • Highly Commended – POP Canberra

Visitor Information Services

  • Winner – Canberra and Region Visitors Centre

Tour and Transport Operators

  • Winner – The Adventure Gene

Adventure Tourism

  • Winner – The Adventure Gene

Tourism Marketing & Campaigns

  • Winner – National Triangle Visitor Map – National Capital Authority
  • Commended – Makers of Murrumbateman

Tourism Wineries, Distilleries & Breweries

  • Winner – The Canberra Distillery
  • Highly Commended – Corang Estate Cellar Door & Pantry
  • Commended – The Vintners Daughter

Caravan and Holiday Parks

  • Winner – Alivio Tourist Park

Hosted Accommodation

  • Winner – The Barn at Nguurruu

3-3.5 Star Accommodation

  • Winner – The Y Canberra Region – Leumeah Lodge

4-4.5 Star Accommodation

  • Winner – Little National Hotel Canberra

5 Star Luxury Accommodation

  • Winner – Hyatt Hotel Canberra – A Park Hyatt Hotel

Excellence in Food Tourism

  • Winner – Murrumbateman Chocolate Co
  • Highly Commended – Haig Park Village Markets

Young Achiever Award

  • Winner – Finn Jeffery
  • Highly Commended – Aaron Hersford

Tourism Visitor Education

  • Winner – Blackwattle Alpaca Farm

Natasha Watson Women in Tourism Award

  • Winner – Dr Naomi Dale.

canberra.title: ACAT decision blow to ACT Revenue Office’s retrospective tax grab
canberra.snippet: The ACT Revenue Office has suffered a humiliating legal defeat that should have wide implications for separated couples caught up in a re...
canberra.content:
20 November 2026

Join the conversation

3

The ACT Revenue Office has faced fierce criticism for the way it operates and deals with taxpayers. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

The ACT Revenue Office has suffered a humiliating legal defeat that should have wide implications for separated couples caught up in a retrospective tax net involving hundreds of thousands of dollars.

The decision in the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal (ACAT) may affect people who sold and bought property due to separation but had been granted a stamp duty concession only for the ACT Revenue Office to reverse its decisions years later.

It is the latest setback for the Territory’s tax collector, which has faced fierce criticism for the way it operates and deals with taxpayers.

Region reported in August that the ACT Revenue Office was facing a clutch of appeals against its retrospective stamp duty assessments, with many involving separated couples angry at how their eligibility for the Home Buyers Concession Scheme had been denied.

Appeals to ACAT flowed after a damning report from the ACT Auditor-General found the ACT Revenue Office failed to explain its complex eligibility requirements, relied on self-assessment and then pursued debtors without regard to their circumstances or financial situation.

It was revealed last year the ACT Revenue Office was chasing thousands of people who had inadvertently filled out their applications for stamp duty concessions incorrectly or were now deemed ineligible, sometimes years later.

The report echoed a Legislative Assembly committee inquiry that found the application process was unclear and the ACT Revenue Office was aggressive and inconsiderate in applying penalties and recovering debts.

Some also accused the Revenue Office of nitpicking and finding technicalities to frustrate the intent of the stamp duty exemption for separating couples forced to sell their shared property and purchase anew as singles.

A recent decision by Senior Member Jennifer Francis found for an applicant who had been retrospectively denied the concession and slugged with $33,845 in duty, including penalty tax ($8,461.25) and interest ($9,158.71).

The assessment came two years after the applicant bought a home in February 2022, 10 months after they sold a property jointly owned with their former partner.

The ACT Revenue Office argued there could not be any concession because the exchange of contracts for the sale of the first home (15 May 2021) and the realisation of the sale in June 2021 occurred before Family Court orders took effect in July 2021.

It said that having been sold before the court orders took effect, the home could not be characterised as an interest required to be relinquished by orders of the Family Court, despite there being an exemption or carve-out for such situations.

But Ms Francis did not agree. “The effect of the respondent’s argument is … to render the court orders nugatory,” she found.

She called the ACT Revenue Office’s position a distraction from the real questions at issue.

The interest in the first home was one that the Family Court orders required to be relinquished. “The fact that the applicant’s interest was sold prior to when the orders of the Family Court were made does not deny … the effect of those orders,” Ms Francis found.

The ACT Revenue Office also argued the proceeds of the sale should be included in the applicant’s gross income, tipping them over the eligibility threshold.

But Ms Francis said the sale of the applicant’s interest in their first home was not a profit-making undertaking.

“The sale was precipitated by their personal circumstances, the separation from their ex-partner,” she said. “Receipt from the realisation of the sale of their interest in their first home is the realisation of a capital asset. It is not income according to ordinary concepts.”

The ACT Revenue Office decision that the applicant was not entitled to stamp duty concession and to impose penalty tax was reversed, and duty and penalty tax paid by the applicant remitted.

canberra.title: ‘Severe’ heatwave to hit coastal communities
canberra.snippet: Residents and visitors along the NSW South Coast are urged to prepare for a three-day heatwave. Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) senior meteor...
canberra.content:
Batemans Bay is expected to bear the brunt of a weekend heatwave. Photo: John Lomnicki.

Residents and visitors along the NSW South Coast are urged to prepare for a three-day heatwave.

Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) senior meteorologist Angus Hines told Region the system will stretch from Sydney’s south, impacting parts of the South Coast hardest.

It’s expected to hit between Kiama and Bermagui, with Batemans Bay, Moruya and Ulladulla forecast to bear the brunt.

“It’s going to be three days of heat … and unusually warm nights, as well,” he said.

In a warning, the BOM urged people to prepare for a severe heatwave.

“Maximum temperatures in the mid 20s to low 30s and overnight minimum temperatures in the mid to high teens [are forecast],” the alert outlines.

“Severe heatwave conditions are expected to develop over the weekend and will peak on Sunday [22 November]. … Locations likely to be impacted include Batemans Bay.”

The BOM is warning of a wet and hot weekend across swaths of southern NSW, with possible storms.

Batemans Bay is set to hover around 31 degrees on Saturday (21 November) and Monday (23 November), but peak at 35 degrees on Sunday.

Moruya is also expected to reach about 30 degrees across the heatwave, alongside towns such as Bermagui, Merimbula and Kiama.

Canberra, at a slightly higher elevation, will escape the worst of the weekend heat.

“It will still be quite warm in Canberra – we’ve got 30 degrees forecast for Sunday and upper 20s surrounding it,” Mr Hines said.

“It’s definitely on the warm side of average.”

North-westerly winds are pushing a hot air mass towards the NSW coast, which is driving the temperature spike.

“That’s likely to be a really strong driving factor,” Mr Hines said of the heatwave.

“That’s a really common weather pattern … in pretty much all the hot days that we get south of Brisbane.”

Mr Hines also said Föhn winds were playing a role, albeit smaller than the north-westerlies.

This weather phenomenon is where hot air rises to pass across mountains and turns into rain before it dries out.

“[During that process], a lot of the water vapour in the air turns into liquid water droplets, that turns into clouds, and that turns into rainfall,” he said.

“The process of turning a gas into a liquid releases heat into the surrounding atmosphere. It might not feel like it when it’s raining, but the surrounding atmosphere gets warmed up.”

But there is relief on the horizon, with the heat expected to peak on Sunday (22 November) before cooling quickly early next week.

“We’re seeing a big wind change move through during the day on Monday,” Mr Hines said.

“We might actually see a notable cooling during Monday, with a windy, rainy change and then eventually some southerlies arriving.”

Mr Hines also said that while this kind of system was “not altogether uncommon” at this time of year, the Bureau was predicting a hot summer.

“This is part of the natural spring cycle, which is quite variable … Just a week ago, we were talking about snow over the Snowies and the Southern Tablelands.

“This is the first of several bursts of heat that most people will experience. It’s likely that we’ll see several more heatwaves.”

You can find the latest warnings from the BOM on its website, while safety tips for enduring a heatwave can be found on the NSW Ambulance website.

Original Article published by Claire Sams on About Regional.

canberra.title: Man accused of hospitalising housemate granted bail despite allegedly saying he ‘would do it again’
canberra.snippet: A court heard a man expressed no remorse after allegedly sending his housemate to hospital with serious injuries, as he apparently told p...
canberra.content:
20 November 2026

Jordan Blake Linning, 24, was granted bail by the ACT Magistrates Court on a charge of assault. Photo: John Lomnicki.

A court heard a man expressed no remorse after allegedly sending his housemate to hospital with serious injuries, as he apparently told police he would assault him all over again.

It is alleged 24-year-old Jordan Blake Linning kicked then punched his housemate in the head at their northern Canberra share home on 2 November 2026.

“The incident was reported to police, and the victim attended hospital for treatment of serious injuries,” an ACT Policing spokesperson said at the time.

Mr Linning handed himself in to police, was charged with assault and spent nearly three weeks in custody before applying for bail in the ACT Magistrates Court on Friday (20 November).

When opposing his bail application, the prosecutor said the housemate reported he would be genuinely fearful if his alleged attacker were released from custody.

The prosecutor also said police thought Mr Linning showed no remorse for the alleged assault. He said when Mr Linning was arrested, he allegedly told police he would do it again and thought he had been justified due to his belief that his housemate was a pedophile.

Special Magistrate Michael Cowen questioned how much weight he could place on these claims by police, because he said they were not contained in any document that had been provided to him for the bail application.

Mr Linning’s lawyer, Tom Tiffen of Hugo Law Group, proposed a strict bail regime, which he argued would alleviate any of the court’s concerns.

He said as the alleged offence took place in a shared accommodation, the plan was for his client to live in a home by himself.

“It appears alcohol was involved in this alleged offence,” he said.

Mr Tiffen said his client had spent 17 days in custody.

“It’s the first time in his life that’s occurred,” he said.

“I understand it’s been a confronting experience.”

Special Magistrate Cowen said the allegations related to “a bizarre set of circumstances”, which may be connected to how Mr Linning had a history of drug-induced psychosis.

But he was satisfied that strict conditions could alleviate the risks of his release and granted bail.

Mr Linning’s bail conditions include not contacting or approaching the housemate, not using alcohol or drugs and being supervised by authorities.

“Yep, I’ll be sent back to jail,” he replied when asked if he understood what would happen if he didn’t comply with his bail conditions.

The matter was adjourned to 3 December.

canberra.title: Planning Authority pauses underdone Hungry Jack’s proposal
canberra.snippet: The development application for a new Hungry Jack’s drive-thru at Koko Molonglo in Wright appears to have been undercooked, with th...
canberra.content:
The bid for a Hungry Jack’s in Wright has hit some planning obstacles. Photo: File

The development application for a new Hungry Jack’s drive-thru at Koko Molonglo in Wright appears to have been undercooked, with the Territory Planning Authority putting the assessment on ice and listing a range of problems.

In pre-decision advice to the proponent, John Krnc’s PK Nominees, the TPA says the DA in its current form would not be approved.

Issues raised include concerns about pedestrian safety, parking, landscaping, lighting and stormwater run-off.

The DA attracted plenty of heat from the Molonglo community, fired up about traffic, litter, noise and potential behaviour concerns.

The single-storey, 279 sqm, 38-seat restaurant and drive-thru are proposed for the corner of Steve Irwin Avenue and Gornall Street, in front of the Aldi supermarket and opposite Wright Children’s Park.

The pre-DA advice says the proposal appears to prioritise vehicles over pedestrians, and does not make a positive contribution to the amenity and character of the surrounding public realm.

It notes that the stand-alone drive-thru is close to existing and future residential development, public open space/playground and key pedestrian routes.

The proposed vehicular access arrangements present an undesirable interface with surrounding public spaces and pedestrian areas, it says.

“As currently presented, it is unclear how the development facilitates safe, convenient and attractive pedestrian movement, particularly where pedestrian routes appear to conflict with multiple vehicle access and egress points,” the advice says.

The TPA is concerned about potential conflicts between drive-thru queuing and vehicles and pedestrians visiting the nearby Aldi and the rest of Koko Molonglo.

Limited pedestrian access along the shopfront and to the main entry may also conflict with vehicles, including those collecting waste, and the proposed tandem staff parking arrangement is not considered optimal.

The proposed site is next to Aldi. The Planning Authority has safety concerns. Image: PK Nominees.

There are concerns about potential conflict between cyclists and vehicles servicing the restaurant because bicycle parking is located next to the loading bay.

The proponent has been asked to review the Traffic Impact Assessment, as well as the site layout to show how it could be made safer.

The proposed nine on-site parking spaces mean the facility is short 19 spaces, with the proponent relying on the existing basement carpark to provide the balance.

But there isn’t enough information to show that existing users won’t be adversely affected.

On lighting, the illuminated signs pose spill problems. The TPA wants to know how they will be managed to minimise potential impacts on surrounding homes, including whether they can be dimmed or switched off outside trading hours.

There are also doubts about whether the landscaping will be enough to mitigate the hard surfaces, and the DA does not say what canopy percentage will be achieved.

The Environmental Protection Agency requires a new Noise Management Plan. Icon Water also cannot support the proposal due to concerns about whether the water and sewerage network will be protected.

The last time the developer proposed a fast food drive-thru, on behalf of KFC in 2019, it was forced to abandon the plans after a community outcry, only for a takeaway shopfront to open in 2025.

The social media reaction to the Hungry Jack’s proposal echoes similar objections.

Some believe another fast food outlet in the area is unwarranted, with McDonald’s and Oporto at North Weston, and the KFC shopfront in Koko.

Others believe traffic will be an issue, particularly given its proximity to a roundabout. They don’t trust the consultant’s view that the road system will easily absorb the extra traffic.

An application to amend the DA will mean the clock restarts on the time it takes to make a decision.

australia.title: Steve Bracks is on board: Ben Carroll finds a believer as most write off Labor’s Victorian election chances
australia.snippet: The former premier arrives to deliver a morale boost as Carroll defends his government’s record and says the royal commission might ‘help...
australia.content:
With Victorian Labor sliding in the polls and the prospect of the premier losing his own seat, the party has turned to a figure from its past for a much-needed morale boost. Climbing aboard Labor’s big red campaign bus on Friday morning was Steve Bracks, the former premier who led the party to three consecutive election victories, including the shock 1999 win that toppled Jeff Kennett’s Coalition government.

“At this stage in 1999, no one gave me a chance to be premier. Kennett looked like he was a shoo-in for that election,” Bracks told reporters at Sunshine hospital.

“There’s still a week to go. It won’t take that much more improvement in our primary vote for us to go very well this election, and that’s the path required.”

But the polls paint a less optimistic picture. Most suggest Labor is facing its worst result in decades, with its primary vote possibly headed for the lowest of any sitting government in Australia since the second world war.

If the party’s primary vote falls as much as is expected, Ben Carroll could become the first Victorian premier to lose his own seat. He holds Niddrie, covering parts of Melbourne’s inner north-west, on a margin of 6.7%. But Carroll this week batted away the idea, arguing that he had strengthened his margin since winning the seat at a 2012 byelection.

Niddrie was among several seats in the region to record significant primary swings against Labor in 2022, although none were lost. Pollsters are now questioning whether the rise of One Nation, polling at about 20% statewide, could change that.

Bracks acknowledged “nothing is safe” in a “three cornered contest election”. But he dismissed suggestions that Labor’s so-called red wall in Melbourne’s west was about to crumble.

“This narrative that somehow Labor is neglecting the west, it’s just totally untrue. Just look at what’s been developed in Melbourne’s west. It’s been revolutionary,” he says, pointing to Sunshine hospital’s new emergency department, the adjacent Joan Kirner Women’s and Children’s hospital and the West Gate tunnel, which opened last year.

“That will hold us in good stead coming to this election, as well. You’re going to be quite surprised and you will see that we will go very well in Melbourne’s west.”

Carroll, who regards Bracks as a mentor, nodded in agreement. Speaking to Guardian Australia, Carroll concedes that after 12 years in government, voters may have begun to take Labor’s achievements for granted.

“We have had to remind them,” he says.

He points to legislated improvements in nurse-to-patient ratios, and cost-of-living measures such as a 20% car registration rebate earlier this year. Then there’s the free kinder funding program for kindergarten children, the Smile Squad dental program for children and a school breakfast program, which has been running since 2016. There’s also support for LGBTQI+ communities, with the deputy premier on Saturday expected to announce $7.5m to continue Victoria’s Pride street party for another four years.

“These are the things that go very quickly from a Liberal government. They get in, and they will look at what they can cut. They’ve done it before,” Carroll says.

The premier says the Coalition has run a small-target campaign, “an empty vessel”, leaving voters with little sense of what the party would actually do in government. He says to achieve a promised cash surplus in 2032, a Coalition government would have to make “significant cuts”.

“I’ve got to make sure that Victorians realise what’s at risk,” Carroll says.

Opposition leader Jess Wilson has previously dismissed the claims as a “desperate scare campaign”, insisting she has no plans to cut frontline services or programs such as the Smile Squad.

Carroll’s response: “You know who also said that? Tony Abbott. And what did he do in his first budget?”

Despite the 2022 swings, Labor picked up an additional seat at the election. At the time, it was seen as a vindication of the government’s response to the Covid pandemic, when Melbourne endured some of the world’s longest lockdowns. But with the benefit of hindsight, Carroll says Labor should have done more to address the “trauma” Victorians suffered during the lockdown.

The state should have “really ramped up” its response to the recommendations of the mental health royal commission, he says, and provided more support for people returning to work and children struggling at school.

He argues the state needs investment in education, health and workers, rather than the infrastructure program pursued by his predecessors.

Unapologetic

It’s been an unforgiving campaign for Carroll. A week before it had even begun, several unions turned their back on Labor, including the Electrical Trades Union. Last election it spent $1.6m on an advertising campaign supporting Labor but this time it said it had to divert its funds to supporting members who could be called before the Big Build royal commission and preparing for an “oncoming attack” from a “majority Coalition government”.

But Carroll is unapologetic about calling the royal commission. It was his first act as premier and he has made it a feature of his election campaign, even putting it on how-to-vote cards.

“I love the trade union movement and I love the Labor party, but I love the state of Victoria even more,” he says. “That was why I called the royal commission.”

The royal commission has held public hearings through the campaign, with Carroll acknowledging some of the evidence has been “uncomfortable”. But he says it is important to “shine a light” on alleged wrongdoing by both unions and contractors.

“I think it might actually help save the labour movement,” Carroll says.

He speaks passionately about the inquiry, as he did during Tuesday’s leaders debate. During that debate, when asked about his predecessors Daniel Andrews’ and Jacinta Allan, Carroll did not refer to them by name, with Wilson taunting him and saying they were “not Voldemort”.

By Friday, Carroll was repeatedly referring to both leaders by name in interviews. Bracks, too, was willing to acknowledge Andrews’ and Allan’s achievements but said their mistakes were “self-evident”.

“There is more work to be done, and Ben’s going to take this up,” he says. “He’s identified where the deficiencies are and what he wants to improve.”

Whether voters are prepared to give Carroll that chance will be clear on 28 November.

australia.title: The politics of sandpapergate - Back to Back Barries podcast
australia.snippet: As early polls open in Victoria, Tony Barry and Barrie Cassidy kick off by taking a look at the Big Build royal commission. They contrast...
australia.content:
As early polls open in Victoria, Tony Barry and Barrie Cassidy kick off by taking a look at the Big Build royal commission. They contrast this inquiry with another investigation making headlines this week – the newly announced forum into who in the Australian cricket team knew sandpaper was being used on the ball back in 2018.

They also examine the prime minister’s summit blitz and wonder whether Albanese is relieved to be far away from Victorian Labor

australia.title: ‘I’m not a dangerous woman’: how retirees Sandra and Marlene became the faces of hate speech laws in Queensland
australia.snippet: As a high court challenge to the controversial ‘river to the sea’ laws looms, Sandra Keller, 75, and Marlene Grace, 72, are the latest in...
australia.content:
Sandra Keller, 75, and Marlene Grace, 72, are the faces of hate speech in Queensland, according to the Crisafulli government. Last week, both retirees were surrounded by police and arrested for “distribution, publication or display of a prohibited symbol”, as was Marlene’s 76-year-old husband, Paul.

For both women it was their first time being arrested. Their crime: carrying a banner that read “from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free” through the streets of Brisbane at a permitted rally last Sunday.

Police allege the two retirees, one a retired mental health counsellor and the other a cardiac nurse, caused a person to feel “menaced, harassed or offended” by their use of the slogan.

They are the latest of more than 40 people arrested, accused of breaching Queensland’s Fighting Antisemitism and Keeping Guns out of the Hands of Terrorists and Criminals Amendment Act 2026.

“I’m the most law-abiding person. I’ve never had a speeding ticket. I’ve never had a parking fine,” Grace said.

“I’m not a dangerous woman. I look after my grandchildren. I’m looking after my grandson today. I look after another one tomorrow. My children wouldn’t have me looking after their children if I was a danger”.

Both vow to do it again.

Keller said she took the action because she was “upset and concerned about the mutilation of children and the destruction in Gaza” and to protest against the legislation for restricting her free speech. Both deny their actions were hateful.

“[The prohibited expression] can’t possibly be hate speech. I wasn’t saying anything hateful against anybody at all,” Keller said.

“Palestinians have a right to live on that land. That’s what that means to me”.

In the eight months since the law went into effect, 37 protesters have been charged for hate speech under the legislation. Others, like Keller and Grace, have been cautioned after their arrest due to a lack of a criminal record.

The oldest is 77, the youngest 18.

Two of the people accused of antisemitic hate speech are Jewish.

Justice for Palestine Magan-djin are challenging the law in the high court, arguing it is an unconstitutional restraint on their right to free expression. On Friday, the matter was briefly mentioned in the high court. The government argues the laws are constitutional. The matter will now likely be heard there in the middle of next year.

Justice for Palestine Magan-djin lead organiser Remah Naji – the lead plaintiff in the high court challenge – said Keller and Grace were ordinary people trying to express their political views peacefully.

“In a context of genocide when people are getting massacred, when hospitals and schools and universities are being bombed and flattened to the ground, we are asking if someone’s words can be harmful to people. I think it’s insane to even think it”

Rushed into law

The attorney general, Deb Frecklington, told parliament earlier this year that there were three elements of the law “which ensure it does not unreasonably limit freedom of expression”.

First, the legislation did not prohibit “expressions which closely resemble a prohibited expression”, just the two common slogans used by the Palestine movement enumerated in the act, Frecklington said

The rarely used slogan “globalise the intifada” is also banned; saying or displaying either is punishable by up to two years’ jail.

That’s only illegal if doing so makes a person feel “menaced, harassed or offended”, something Frecklington described as a “high bar,” citing a high court case that found that the clause only banned conduct “calculated or likely to arouse significant anger, significant outrage, disgust or hatred in the mind of a reasonable person in all the circumstances”.

It is also not illegal to use the slogan to argue against its use.

Third, the act also establishes a range of defences allowing people to say the banned words for genuine artistic, religious, educational or historical purpose, or in the public interest, such as during a “genuine public dispute”.

Passed in response to the Bondi terrorist attack, after months of behind-the-scenes work, the legislation was rushed into law in March, with just seven days set aside for public comment.

In response to a right to information request by the Guardian for documents relating to the Bondi terrorist attack or the development of the legislation, the department found more than 125 folios of documents but has been banned from releasing any of them for 10 years on the basis that they are cabinet documents, a practice that was heavily criticised by the government in opposition.

The law has proved remarkably easy to evade for those who want to. Protesters routinely turn up to rallies with the banned slogan written in Swedish or Indonesian, replace a single word in the sentence with a rhyming one or reverse the order of “river” and “sea” to chant it legally.

But they haven’t protected everyone.

The Guardian has observed two protesters being threatened with arrest for signs bearing the wrong expression.

Many have claimed a defence, such as Liam Parry, who used the slogan to explain what he said was its history at a rally in March. He was arrested and charged anyway. At most rallies, every person using the expressions is arrested.

Keller said one of the great ironies is that many of the arrests have taken place at Brisbane’s Emma Miller Place, a park in the city CBD.

It is named for a suffragist who was so outraged by a brutal police crackdown on peaceful protesters during the 1912 Brisbane general strike that she assaulted police commissioner William Cahill with a hatpin, causing him to be thrown off his horse. She was 72.

Keller said she was inspired by women like Miller and Merle Thornton, a feminist honoured with a statue this week for chaining herself to a Brisbane bar to fight for an equal right to drink.

“I wanted to stand up just the same as those women, for what I believe in. I have that right,” she said.

australia.title: As the Coalition stares down One Nation in NSW, a new threat is rising: the teals
australia.snippet: The opposition’s struggle is creating an opportunity for progressive independents who are boosted by shrewd political operator Chris Minn...
australia.content:
The New South Wales Coalition is facing a renewed threat to its heartland seats on Sydney’s north shore.

This time, the threat is from independent candidates – and they’re backed by the same community activists who put a swathe of teal independents into federal parliament.

The challenge, which has so far remained under the radar, comes as the NSW Coalition tries to shore up its right flank against a surging One Nation before the March state election. This has resulted in the Coalition lurching to the right on issues ranging from gun control to law and order, and, in the case of the NSW Nationals, to abandon climate targets altogether.

As former opposition leader Mark Speakman resigned from the Liberals on Thursday – joining an exodus of MPs announcing they wouldn’t contest their seats in March – he warned his party against becoming “One Nation lite”.

But the move to the right has also created an opportunity for progressive independents running in urban seats usually held by Liberal moderates, with several candidates about to launch their campaigns.

This weekend, Amelia Loye, a management consultant who specialises in stakeholder and community engagement, will announce she is running in the seat of Willoughby, on Sydney’s north shore. She will attempt to oust Liberal MP Tim James, who holds the seat on a 2.6% margin.

Loye is backed by community group Willoughby Votes, which came close to securing an independent in the 2023 election with 47% of the two-party preferred vote.

“Willoughby has already shown it is ready for an independent,” she said. “Nearly half of voters backed one last time. I want to earn their support, and the support of those still deciding.”

She joins high-profile candidate Elouise Massa, a small business owner, who became a household name after campaigning for Northern Beaches hospital to return to public hands after her toddler’s death in emergency.

Massa will run in the Sydney seat of Manly against Liberal Adelaide Cuneo, who is seeking to replace the retiring MP, James Griffin.

The independent deputy mayor of Mosman, Michael Randall, announced last weekend he will run in North Shore as a community independent. Several of the people behind former independent federal MP Kylea Tink’s campaign are supporting him.

Monica Wulff, another independent, has announced a run in Davidson.

Voters on the northern beaches have already sent two independents to Macquarie street – and both have a good chance of being returned.

At the federal level, teal independents Sophie Scamps, Zali Steggall and Nicolette Boele hold McKellar, Warringah and Bradfield respectively. Tink held North Sydney for one term before the seat was abolished.

The NSW Liberal party is not giving up on the northern beaches and the north shore, despite the trend towards independents.

“We’ll keep making our case directly to voters, including why we oppose Labor’s gun buyback that targets law-abiding owners rather than criminals and terrorists,” a Liberal spokesperson said.

This time, however, the independents have a boost in the form of NSW Labor premier, Chris Minns.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

During the final weeks of parliament before the NSW election, Minns joked that independent Jacqui Scruby, who won Pittwater at a byelection, should be known as “the member for Mona Vale road” for her tenacity in seeking an upgrade. It’s now being fast-tracked by the Minns government.

Minns has also appeared with Massa, and praised her for her advocacy.

But Minns, a shrewd political operator, has not fallen in love with independents – he’s just hedging his bets.

A year ago, with the Liberals languishing in the polls, Labor could have expected to increase its majority in 2027. But with One Nation storming to a primary vote as high as 30% in some polls, that prospect has dimmed.

In the current parliament, Labor has support of three independents – Greg Piper, Joe McGirr and Alex Greenwich – to ensure confidence and supply for its minority government. An expanded crossbench would give more options and provide a buffer for Labor losses to One Nation in western Sydney, the Hunter and possibly the Central Coast.

If all independents were successful – and that is a big if – almost the entire north shore region would go to state independents, except the seat of Wahroonga.

Most of the commentary about the 2027 election has focused on the likely Armageddon facing the Nationals, who could lose as many eight or nine of their 11 seats in the regions.

But a teal wave also remains a threat to the Liberal party, especially as the Coalition try to position themselves to fight off One Nation in the regions with policies that don’t sit well with urban voters.

One Nation could also prove helpful to independents if it makes good on its promise to run candidates in every seat. The party is more likely to shave votes from the Liberal primary vote, making it easier for the independents to overtake the Liberal on preferences from Labor and the Greens.

NSW’s optional preferential voting makes it hard to predict how strong flows will be – and it depends what parties advocate on how to votes. But in 2023 only 41% of One Nation voters nominated preferences, compared to 70% of Green voters and 49% of Labor voters.

The opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, has not ruled out either a preference deal or a post-election arrangement with One Nation, describing such options as “hypothetical”. But if they do end up preferencing One Nation, it may alienate moderate Liberals and ultimately work against them.

  • Disclosure: Anne Davies worked as a media and policy adviser to the independent federal MP Sophie Scamps from October 2023 to October 2024.

australia.title: ‘It gives me power’: the swimming class that’s changing lives
australia.snippet: People who arrive in Australia not having learned to swim often fear the water. For these Splash of Colour students, even blowing bubbles...
australia.content:
In a public pool in Melbourne’s west, where the smell of chlorine hangs thick in the air, Dharmveer Kaur practises blowing bubbles in the shallow pool. Sounds echo across the enormous indoor aquatic centre, as people fresh from school and work mingle in the pools, spas and water slides. Kaur quietly concentrates on submerging her face in the water, following her instructor’s guidance in a lane away from the chaos.

To the young children taking swimming lessons in the lane beside her, the throngs of older men making their way to the spa, or the mother casually breastfeeding in the pool opposite her, Kaur’s bubble blowing may not seem remarkable. But for the woman who never learned to swim, it feels monumental.

When the 37-year-old started swimming lessons three months ago, she was nervous to even enter the pool.

“I had a little bit of [anxiety] putting my mouth into the water,” she says. “I told the teachers my situation and I’m slowly getting confident to breathe in water.”

After moving to Melbourne from the landlocked Indian state of Punjab in 2020, Kaur was struck by the way Melburnians regularly headed to beaches and pools to socialise. Her inability to join in felt like a barrier to more than just the water.

“I was very hesitant to be around people in the water,” she says. “I [was] losing my confidence and then that comes up in different things, like, how do I talk to others, to come in confidently, to be in the groups?”

When her daughter turned six months old, Kaur worried she wouldn’t be able to take her swimming, potentially passing on her fear of water and risking similar social exclusion. But the prospect of attending lessons alone, the cost and her husband’s doubt initially held her back.

Kaur eventually found A Splash of Colour Swimming, a program for culturally and linguistically diverse adults learning to swim. The lessons were free, at a time of day when her daughter was in day care, and with other adult women at the nearby AquaPulse Centre in Hoppers Crossing.

For Kaur, the lessons have become as much about finding independence and community as learning to swim. Initially, her husband was reluctant to support her attending lessons; in their home town women were not encouraged to learn the skill.

“He was not giving me the car keys,” she says. “And so I said, ‘No, I have to go’. In that way, it gives me power and encouragement to get out of home for myself.”

It was the other women in the class who helped Kaur persevere.

“If I was doing this alone, with the barriers I was feeling at home, I don’t think I could have coped,” she says. “But I have my group. We have a class, and that was an excitement. I was like, ‘They are my people’.”

The founder of A Splash of Colour Swimming, Ennia Jones, says fear and a lack of self-confidence are common barriers among people who arrive in Australia without having learned to swim.

According to Royal Life Saving Australia, people born overseas account for one in three drowning deaths in Australia. Last year 313 people drowned across the country, 10% above the 10-year average. A report by the Australian Water Safety Council identified declining swimming skills, particularly among multicultural communities, as a contributing factor to the rise in drowning deaths.

Jones knows first-hand how deeply ingrained a fear of water can become. Having grown up in Zimbabwe without knowing how to swim, she only learned at 12 years old thanks to a school principal determined to break the intergenerational avoidance among younger Zimbabweans.

“One of the patterns we see in our program is that when parents have never learned to swim, uncertainty or fear around water can unintentionally be passed on to their children. Over time, avoiding the water can become normal within a family or community.”

It was only after moving to Newcastle and taking up lap swimming as an adult that she really fell in love with the water, seeing the benefits it provided her wellbeing. But she also noticed the lack of cultural diversity in public pools.

She began asking people within her own African community why they did not swim. She found many had never learned, and had come to fear the water, had concerns about swimwear, and faced barriers to finding the time and money for lessons.

Jones established A Splash of Colour as a response to what she had learned. She was pleasantly surprised when the first group was oversubscribed.

What started as a program of 20 women three years ago in Newcastle has now grown to between 300 and 500 people a week learning to swim across New South Wales, Victoria, the ACT and Queensland. The average participant is 55 years old, and the oldest is a 71-year-old woman determined to swim with her grandchildren.

The program supplies caps, goggles and swimming bags, and takes students on virtual tours of shops to show them where they can buy modest swimwear.

“If you’ve got braids like I do, finding a swimming cap in an ordinary store can be incredibly difficult. I once tried squeezing my braids into two standards caps. It was a disaster, and my hair still took ages to dry,” Jones says.

“Providing swimming caps that are actually designed for different hair volumes has made an enormous difference for our participants.”

It is important, she says, to allow people to approach the water at their own pace. For some, even getting in the water and blowing bubbles “is Everest”, says Jones. Before lessons begin, participants take part in ‘Brave Beginnings’ where they are given workbooks exploring water trauma, learn about swimming etiquette and are encouraged to gradually familiarise themselves with the water.

At the second-last class of term, Kelisha Veerasamy, 34, sits on the benches in the stuffy aquatic centre. Despite having a cold that prevents her from swimming, she has shown up to encourage the other women she’s developed friendships with over the 10-week course.

Veerasamy moved to Melbourne from South Africa four years ago. Learning to swim has been another step in establishing her new life.

“To learn a new skill can be quite overwhelming when you’re trying to learn everything else that was once normal for you,” she says.

She says the group of women helped remove the embarrassment she once associated with being an adult beginner. The women applaud when someone masters a new technique and encourage each other to persevere.

“There’s no judgment there,” she says.

Veerasamy says being confident in the water has opened up an “unexplored world”, helping her feel more connected to the Australian outdoors.

“I feel like we’ve integrated a lot more into the Australian culture and with the water,” she says. “We’ve already been taking my son to the beach, to splash in pools, and I want to jump in with him.”

The manager of the AquaPulse pool, Stacey Mancer, says watching participants become more comfortable in the water has been one of the most rewarding aspects of the program.

“This is why I do this job,” she says. “You may not be creating Olympic swimmers, but just building some confidence and some education about water safety is so important.”

Mancer says it’s important for swimming facilities to cater to diverse communities so as to continue operating as equalisers, accessible to all who want to enjoy the water.

At one centre Mancer worked at, the prime minister came to swim alongside locals who lived in the nearby housing commissions. “That’s the demographic you can get in a pool,” she says.

“Everyone wants to swim.”

world.title: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
world.snippet: Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded Multiple coastal hazard warnings we...
world.content:
Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.

After a yellow level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

world.title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
world.snippet: The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits Environmentalists in South Afri...
world.content:
Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.

The case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.

The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.

Otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”

Sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, said she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted quickly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.

“As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.

The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.

Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.

“A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”

Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.

The trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”

Baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.

The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” said Venter.

A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.

Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

world.title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
world.snippet: Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds One in four women around ...
world.content:
One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.

“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”

The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.

“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.

He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.

In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.

Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.

Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”

She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.

“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”

world.title: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
world.snippet: A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza Fears are growing that the US could impose ...
world.content:
Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.

It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.

The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.

The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.

The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.

The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.

The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.

Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.

Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians.”

In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”

In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”

He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.

Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.

In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically”.

It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.

The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of The Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.

The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.

Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.

On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

world.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
world.snippet: Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans The European Commission has been a...
world.content:
The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.

Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.

The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.

Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.

In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.

If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).

According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.

In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.

“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”

Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.

The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.

The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.

One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.

In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.

The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.

In order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers shows that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.

On this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU announced the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.

The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.

During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.

Timothy Kaldas, the deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, said the commission had generally “done a poor job of leveraging the funds of European taxpayers to support genuine stabilisation” on the other side of the Mediterranean. “The strategic interest of Europe is seeing a more economically stable Egypt with a population that is less precarious,” he said.

Sandra Gómez López, a Spanish socialist MEP who recently visited Cairo to assess human rights in Egypt, said the data presented by the Guardian raised important questions. “The commission must explain transparently why it considers these commitments to have been fulfilled and demonstrate that European funding is genuinely contributing to improving social protection for the Egyptian population,” she said.

She stressed that the EU should not withdraw support, “but neither can we allow the country’s strategic importance to lead us to lower our standards when it comes to human rights”.

For critics, the questions about the EU’s willingness to hold Egypt accountable on very precise socioeconomic targets do not bode well for the broader but less defined goals for democracy and human rights.

Strik said: “The fact that Egypt and the commission even seem to ignore the crystal-clear socioeconomic conditions doesn’t increase my expectation that they adhere to the vague precondition on democracy and the rule of law.”

Claudio Francavilla, an associate EU director at Human Rights Watch, said: “Without benchmarks, the EU has turned a human rights conditionality into a blank cheque for Egypt’s authoritarianism.”

In a statement to the Guardian, the European Commission said the policy target on Takaful and Karama referred to new beneficiary families “and not to its net increase”. The spokesperson said there was “no contradiction” between this statement and that in a confidential document that said Egypt was required to “further expand cash transfer programmes”.

Asked about the release of the remaining €1.5bn in promised loans, the commission said it “will be made once all conditions have been met”, referring to 24 economic policy conditions, keeping an IMF programme on track and “taking concrete and credible steps towards respecting effective democratic mechanisms, including a multiparty parliamentary system, and the rule of law, and guaranteeing respect for human rights”.

It added: “Compliance with the conditionality is examined thoroughly” by EU officials and diplomats based on “information provided by the Egyptian authorities and other relevant sources”.

Egypt’s mission to the EU in Brussels did not respond to a request for comment.
